messages.body_plain:
Thanks Terry. Just to be sure, I changed a bit my script and model specs., and used the "std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE" as you suggested:

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

library("lavaan", lib.loc="~/R/win-library/3.2")

# define Pop model

mPopModel <- '
# outer model

CO =~ CO1
EU =~ 0.8*EU1 + 0.8*EU2 + 0.8*EU3 + 0.8*EU4 + 0.8*EU5

GT =~ 0.6*GT1 + 0.6*GT2 + 0.7*GT3 + 0.7*GT4 + 0.8*GT5
AC =~ 0.5*AC1 + 0.6*AC2 + 0.6*AC3 + 0.7*AC4 + 0.7*AC5
SU =~ 0.55*SU1 + 0.6*SU2 + 0.65*SU3 + 0.7*SU4 + 0.75*SU5
# inner model

EU ~ 0.418*CO
GT ~ 0.515*CO
AC ~ 0.288*CO
SU ~ 0.0*CO + 0.157*EU + 0.542*GT + 0.254*AC
'

# generate data based on Pop model
mData <- simulateData(mPopModel,sample.nobs=10000L,
                      standardized=TRUE)

# define analysis model

mModel <- '
# outer model

CO =~ CO1
EU =~ EU1 + EU2 + EU3 + EU4 + EU5

GT =~ GT1 + GT2 + GT3 + GT4 + GT5
AC =~ AC1 + AC2 + AC3 + AC4 + AC5

SU =~ SU1 + SU2 + SU3 + SU4 + SU5
# inner model
EU ~ CO

GT ~ CO
AC ~ CO

SU ~ CO + EU + GT + AC
'

# analyze data
mFit <- sem(mModel,data=mData,std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)
summary(mFit,nd=4,standardized=T,fit.measures=T,rsquare=T) # show std solution

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Still, I got results similar to the ones I had before - in terms of messed up estimates. For example:

Regressions:

  EU ~

  GT ~
    CO                0.3455    0.0112   30.8270    0.0000    0.3266    0.3266
  AC ~
    CO                0.1943    0.0115   16.9057    0.0000    0.1907    0.1907
  SU ~
    CO                0.0307    0.0154    1.9881    0.0468    0.0210    0.0210
    EU                0.2690    0.0148   18.1983    0.0000    0.1909    0.1909
    GT                0.8411    0.0200   41.9680    0.0000    0.6094    0.6094
    AC                0.3686    0.0168   21.9949    0.0000    0.2571    0.2571

Looking at the values under the Std.lv column, the following regressions are too far off the true values: EU ~ CO,  GT ~ CO, and  AC ~ CO.

With a sample size of 10K, these regressions should be a lot closer to the true values than they are. That is what motivated my original post.

Now, I think you are correct that this is not due to endogeneity, because the analysis model is correctly specified vis-a-vis the population model.

Maybe something missing in the settings of the sem() function, in addition to the "std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE" you mentioned?

messages.body_plain:
I'm currently doing a multigroup cfa of a bifactor model with 65 items and 14 specific factors. I'm running a configural invariance model, then I'm constraining the model through the group.equal argument, including loadings (metric invariance) and then loadings and intercepts together (scalar invariance).

I noticed that when loadings are constrained, the degrees of freedom increase by 115, which makes sense: 51 df for the specific factors and 64 df for the general factor.

However, when intercepts are also constrained for scalar invariance, the degrees of freedom increase only by 50 in total. I would have expected an increase of 115 df. This makes me wonder if some of the intercepts are not being constrained.

I only get this type of issue when testing hierarchical models (e.g. bifactor and higher-order). For simple (lower-order) models, the degrees of freedom gained are the same with metric and scalar invariance.

Any thoughts?

Thank you for all your work.

Ylenio

messages.subject: Re: modification indices do not include intercepts
messages.subject_clean: modification indices do not include intercepts
messages.body_plain:
On 11/24/2015 03:31 PM, Bunga Citra Pratiwi Asnawi wrote:
> With the new version of the lava an package the modification indices
> could not return intercepts.
>

> /mo <- modindices(strong.fit)/

This is due to a change in 0.5-19. From the release notes:

"the function modindices() will now only show modification indices for
newly added parameters; to assess the impact of releasing equality
constraints, use the function lavTestScore()"

So 'modindices()' now only shows modification indices for 'new'
parameters that were not included in the original model. It does not
show modification indices for (equality)-constrained parameters. In your
example, the intercepts were constrained by the group.equal="intercepts"
argument.

To see the effect of 'releasing' these equality constraints, you should
use the (new) lavTestScore() function. This will give you a 'global'
(multivariate) score test (aka the Lagrange Multiplier test), as well as
univariate and cumulative score tests for releasing a single constraint
at a time. Finally, you can also see how the other variables of the
model will change, if you release all the constraints.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
> Can you elaborate why one cannot estimate the individual values of M* and Y*? How is the mean and SD of M* otherwise estimated?

They aren't.  The mean/SD of the underlying distribution are assumed fixed by necessity, usually to be standard normal (mu = 0, sigma = 1; this is the "delta" parameterization), but instead of assuming the total variance of M* is 1, you could assume the residual variance of M* is 1 (this is called the "theta" parameterization).  Using one of those assumptions, the thresholds are estimated as the z-scores corresponding the the cumulative probabilities implied by the observed sample proportions in each category.  You see values for the (residual) variances and (total) scales of y* (i.e., the SD of M* and Y*) in the lavaan summary output, but no standard errors because they are fixed rather than estimated.

You can estimate the M and SD of the latent responses in situations such as multigroup or longitudinal models, where you constrain thresholds to be equal over time or across groups (to test strong measurement invariance), and any difference in the observed sample proportions in each category is assumed to be due to differences/changes in the M/SD of the latent response(s).  Here are a couple of places you can start reading:

http://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

http://ibg.colorado.edu/cdrom2012/boomsma/FactorAnalysis/PracticalMeasurementInvarianceOrdinal/Literature/Millsap2004.pdf

Terry

messages.subject_clean: Model identification, possible null B matrix?
messages.body_plain:
> model1<-'Y1~X1
> Y2~X1+Y1
> Y3~X1+Y1'
>
> This model is under-identified.

No, it is just-identified (df = 0), not underidentified (df < 0).

> However, if modified as follows
>
> model1<-'Y1~X1
> Y2~X1+Y1
> Y3~X1+Y1+ Y2*0'
>
> the model is over-identified and can be solved.

The just-identified model can also be solved.  There is just no way to assess fit with df = 0 because fit is arbitrarily perfect.

> Both models have the same # of fixed and free parameters.

That depends on the function you use, because you haven't specified all your model parameters in your model syntax.  Only if the first model does not include the residual covariance(s) among outcomes (here, Y2 and Y3) are the models equivalent, but that would also mean the first model is over-identified.  By default, lavaan will include those residual covariances if you use the sem() function.  If you use the lavaan() function, that default is turned off, but you have to specify all your parameters (including residual variances) for the correct model to run -- or you can turn on the "auto.var = TRUE" option to automatically estimate all (residual) variances.

> Seemingly because the path between Y2 and Y3 is unspecified in model 1 there could be a null B matrix making the model just-identified?

No, the Beta matrix would not be null just because one element is fixed to zero.  You syntax is freely estimating 5 other elements of the B matrix.

> Finally, I am unsure about applying the t-rule. Are there 9 unique elements in both models?

That depends if you treat X1 as a fixed covariate or as another random variable in your model.  If you set "fixed.x = FALSE" in your call to lavaan() or sem(), then you are analyzing a 4-by-4 covariance matrix with 10 unique moments, so you can only estimate up to 10 unknowns (9 if you want to test fit).  To count the number of free parameters, you could use the lavaanify() function to transform your syntax into a parameter table, so you can see which parameters will be estimated based on your syntax, but make sure you set the arguments in lavaanify() to match the arguments you use when you call lavaan() -- or the lavaan() defaults that are set in the sem() function.

> model1 <- 'Y1 ~ X1
> Y2 ~ X1 + Y1
> Y3 ~ X1 + Y1'
> lavaanify(model1, auto.var = TRUE, fixed.x = FALSE) # for example

Anything row that does not have 0 in the "free" column is a freely-estimated parameter.

Terry

Many thanks!

Am Freitag, 23. Oktober 2015 10:22:58 UTC+2 schrieb Terrence Jorgensen:

> > Model1  <- '
> >
> > #define latent variables
> >
> > Latent1 =~ x1+x2+x3
> >
> > Latent2 =~ x4+x5+x6
> >
> > Latent3 =~ x7+x8
> >
> > Latent4 =~ x9+x10
> >
> > #define structural relations
> >
> > Latent1 ~ Latent2
> >
> > Latent3 ~ Latent1 + Latent2
> >
> > Latent4 ~ Latent1 + Latent2 + Latent3
> >
> > x2 ~~ x3
> >
> > '
>

> I know this isn't your question, but... Your Latent1 factor is already just-identified with only 3 indicators.  Adding a residual correlation between two of the indicators might make it empirically under-identified.  I'm not sure whether embedding that measurement model within a larger model makes it identified, but it might be the case -- that is the case for the 2-indicator factors (whose parameters would be under-identified on their own, but are identified in a larger model with simple structure).

>
> > Because most indicator variables are ordinal (Likert 4-scale) I proceed like this:
>

> In order to establish strong invariance, all location parameters in the measurement model must be constant across groups.  The intercepts apply only to your continuous indicators (x8 - x10).  You also need to test the threshold constraints for x1 - x7.  You can do this at the same time as intercepts:
>
> > 2. Weak                      ("loadings")
> >
> > 3. Strong                     ("loadings","intercepts","thresholds")
>
> Or you can do so in separate steps (the order doesn't matter).
>
> > 2. Weak                      ("loadings")
> >
> > 3. Strong(1)               ("loadings","intercepts")
> >
> > 4. Strong(2)               ("loadings","intercepts","thresholds")
>
>
> >
> > 5. Structural                      ("loadings","intercepts","means","regressions")
>
> In order for structural regressions to be comparable across groups, the latent variables need to be on the same scale, so you need to first test those restrictions:
>
> > 5. Structural scale                ("loadings","intercepts","thresholds","means","lv.variances")
> > 6. Structural relations          ("loadings","intercepts","thresholds","means","lv.variances","regressions")
>
> If you can't constrain the latent (residual) variances to equality, you can still compare structural regressions by using phantom variables.  Essentially, for each latent (residual) variance that can't be constrained, you define a second-order factor with variance fixed to 1, the residual variance of the first order factor fixed to zero, and freely estimate the "loading" (beta path), which will be the square root of your original latent (residual) variance.  Then, you estimate regressions among the phantom variables, which are on the same (standardized) scale.  If you need to implement this, here is a paper that employs that rather clever trick:
>
> http://agencylab.ku.edu/~agencylab/manuscripts/(Card%20and%20Little.in%20press.%20-%20SEM%20and%20agg).pdf

>
> > To evaluate invariance I would primarily look at cfi values, because of the dwls estimator and the rather large sample size. I would use cfi cutoff value from Meade et al. (2008) of .002.
>

> Careful, that study was based on continuous data.  The CFI is calculated from chi-squared, so I'm not sure why you think DWLS invalidates one but not the other.  Certainly the large sample sizes will make the chi-squared sensitive to trivial differences, but read this recent paper about using change in CFI with ordinal indicators:
>
> http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2014.882658

>
>
> > 1.     1. Is it defensible to report latent mean differences, even there is no decrease of the model fit (cfi in particular) between model 3 (Strong) and model 4 (Mean)?
>

> Not really, that's the point of testing the constraints.  The null hypothesis is that those parameters do not differ across groups, and you failed to reject that null hypothesis.  But remember, your comparison was not valid because you failed to constrain thresholds, so those differences in thresholds may have absorbed the misspecification of equal means if the null is really false.  So there is still hope for rejection once you update your method :-)

>
> > 2.     2. Is it defensible to assume a moderation effect, because of the decrease of cfi between model 4 (Mean) and Model 5 (Structural) concerning Meade`s (2008) cfi cutoff value?
>

> See my note above about putting latent variables on the same scale across groups before making inferences about whether regression paths actually differ across groups.  But once you update your method, yes, rejecting the null hypothesis of equal regression slopes means that the magnitude of at least one slope depends on group (i.e., interaction / moderation).
>
> Terry

Indeed. Without full data, you can not compute WLS.V. If the correlation
matrix came to you as 'given', and you have no access to the original
data that was used to create it, you can not use lavaan using WLS and
friends. At best, you can treat the data as continuous, use ML, and get
suboptimal results.

That is not an easy task. And it requires full data. The canonical
reference is Muthen 1984.

There are various ways to compute this WLS.V matrix, and that is the
reason why we have this WLS.V argument: to study the effect of different
WLS.V flavors on the quality of the estimates/inference.

Yves.

Oh dear. Another victim of the 'predict()' confusion. In 0.5-19, I
expanded the documentation of lavPredict() a bit, and I added to the
'details' section the following:

"If there are no latent variables in the model, ‘type = "ov"’ will
      simply return the values of the observed variables. Note that this
      function can not be used to `predict' values of dependent
      variables, given the values of independent values (in the
      regression sense). In other words, the structural component is
      completely ignored (for now)."

Example:

 > fit <- sem('y1 ~ x1 + x2; y2 ~ y1', data = PoliticalDemocracy)
 > head( lavPredict(fit, type="yhat") )
         y1       y2       x1       x2
[1,]  2.50 0.000000 4.442651 3.637586
[2,]  1.25 0.000000 5.384495 5.062595
[3,]  7.50 8.800000 5.961005 6.255750
[4,]  8.90 8.800000 6.285998 7.567863
[5,] 10.00 3.333333 5.863631 6.818924
[6,]  7.50 3.333333 5.533389 5.135798

      y1       y2       x1       x2
1  2.50 0.000000 4.442651 3.637586
2  1.25 0.000000 5.384495 5.062595
3  7.50 8.800000 5.961005 6.255750
4  8.90 8.800000 6.285998 7.567863
5 10.00 3.333333 5.863631 6.818924
6  7.50 3.333333 5.533389 5.135798

The very purpose of lavPredict() is to `predict' latent variable scores
(aka factor scores). It is (currently) not very useful in the
observed-variables-only setting.

In the latent variable setting, the purpose of type="ov" (or
type="yhat") is to compute the model-implied (continuous) values for the
observed indicators, once we have computed the model-implied latent
variable scores.

If you need predictions in the regression sense, you will need to
compute them manually.

A late reply:

MLR is Mplus speak for 'robust' ML. This means that the estimation is
vanilla ML, but the inference (standard error, goodness of fit) is robust.

So, when we only talk about estimation, MLR is just plain ML.

MML is also ML, but refers to a specific approach that is used in the
context of categorical data. In this setting, can either 'integrate out'
the latent response (y*) variables (this is estimator = FML, but totally
useless), or we can integrate out the latent variables; the latter is
(in the IRT literature) usually called 'marginal ML'

Mplus calls this 'ML(R)', but lavaan does not.

In lavaan, MML can only be used in the categorical setting (with latent
variables), while ML(R) can only be used in the continuous setting.

Yves.

For future reference:

Since 0.5-20, the function modindices() only gives modification indices
for 'newly added' parameters: parameters that were not included in the
original model, or parameters that were fixed to a constant (say, zero).

For (equality) constraints (either explicit constraints, using labels or
the == operator, or via the group.equal= argument) you should use the
lavTestScore() function, which provides score tests (aka Lagrange
Multiplier tests) for releasing all the constraints in the model
(multivariate), one constraint at a time (univariate), or releasing
constraints in a cumulative fashion. It also provides EPC values for all
the other parameters in the model, if all (or a selection of) the
constraints are released.

(Remember: for adding new parameters, modification indices are identical
to the test statistics of univariate score tests)

messages.subject: Re: WLS.V
messages.subject_clean: WLS.V
messages.body_plain:
First thing you should know is that WLS.V is the (inverse) of the
asymptotic variance matrix of the *sample statistics*. It has nothing
to do with 'observation weights'. Think of it as 'sample statistics
weights'.

So if you have, say 5 binary observed variables (and no x-covariates),
the sample statistics are: 5*(5-1)/2 = 10 correlations, and 5
thresholds. The dimension of WLS.V will be 15 x 15.

Small example:

# create binary version of Holzinger & Swineford data
HS9 <- HolzingerSwineford1939[,c("x1","x2","x3","x4","x5",
                                  "x6","x7","x8","x9")]
HSbinary <- as.data.frame( lapply(HS9, cut, 2, labels=FALSE) )

# 5 binary observed variables
model <- ' trait =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 '

# use estimator "WLS" to show the full weight matrix
fit <- cfa(model, data=HSbinary, ordered=names(HSbinary), std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,
            estimator = "WLS")
inspect(fit, "WLS.V")

In lavaan (0.5-20), the first 5 rows/cols correspond with the
thresholds, the last 10 rows/cols correspond with the correlations. When
estimator = "DWLS" (the default), only the diagonal of this weight
matrix is used.

Yves.

messages.subject_clean: Bias in Weighted Least Squares Estimates
messages.body_plain:
On 08/17/2015 08:25 PM, Michael Hunter wrote:
> Hi Lavaan Users and Developers!
>
> I'm a developer on the OpenMx SEM project.  One of the things I've been
> working lately is weighted least squares (WLS).  I've noticed an odd
> behavior for WLS when there are both ordinal (categorical) and
> continuous variables.  In this case, using the full WLS produces
> positively biased estimates, but the estimates from diagonally WLS or
> ULS are fine.

Hello Michael.

Four months later, I (re)discover this interesting post. (In August, I
saw your post, thought it was interesting, and then -in true vacation
modus- forgot all about it.)

There is indeed bias when using WLS for your model/data combination, but
I think this is not due to a 'bug' in the software (or the methodology).
Reassuringly, Mplus gives exactly the same results as lavaan. For the
skeptics, I attach the dataset (mplus.raw, N=10000), and the mplus
input/output files, as well as the the lavaan output in lavaan_output.txt).

(As to why the numbers between OpenMx and lavaan are slightly different,
this is mostly a matter of how exactly the weight matrix is computed.
Different approaches are possible, and lavaan and OpenMx use slightly
different strategies. I do not think this matters much.)

As was correctly pointed out by Stas, the reason for the 'bias' in this
case is model misspecification! WLS is much less forgiving if the model
is misspecified, compared to DWLS/ULS and even ML. When the model is
closer to the data, the bias goes away. For example:

library(lavaan)
pop.model <- 'f =~ 0.7*y1 + 0.7*y2 + 0.7*y3 + 0.5*y4 + 0.5*y5 + 0.5*y6'
Data <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs = 10000L, standardized = TRUE)
fit <- sem('f =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + y6', data = Data, estimator =
"WLS")
summary(fit, standardized = TRUE)
lavaan (0.5-20) converged normally after  16 iterations

   Number of observations                         10000

   Estimator                                        WLS
   Minimum Function Test Statistic                5.453
   Degrees of freedom                                 9
   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.793

Parameter Estimates:

   Information                                 Expected
   Standard Errors                             Standard

Latent Variables:
                    Estimate  Std.Err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
   f =~
     y1                1.000                               0.704    0.700
     y2                0.990    0.017   56.930    0.000    0.697    0.702
     y3                0.987    0.017   57.738    0.000    0.695    0.702
     y4                0.696    0.016   42.546    0.000    0.490    0.492
     y5                0.688    0.016   41.815    0.000    0.484    0.486
     y6                0.716    0.016   44.082    0.000    0.504    0.504

Note also that this 'bias' has nothing to do with the
categorical/continuous combination. If we only use continuous data, we
observe the same bias. Using your data generation script:

cDat  <- rmvnorm(10000, sigma=sigma)
jdat2 <- data.frame(cDat, scale(cDat+rnorm(prod(dim(cDat)))))
names(jdat2) <- c("y1","y2","y3","y4","y5","y6")

fit <- sem('f =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + y6', data = jdat2, estimator =
"WLS", meanstructure = TRUE)

 > summary(fit, standardized = TRUE)
lavaan (0.5-20) converged normally after  26 iterations

   Number of observations                         10000

   Estimator                                        WLS
   Minimum Function Test Statistic             5224.324
   Degrees of freedom                                 9
   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.000

Parameter Estimates:

   Information                                 Expected
   Standard Errors                             Standard

Latent Variables:
                    Estimate  Std.Err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
   f =~
     y1                1.000                               0.766    0.841
     y2                0.972    0.014   71.063    0.000    0.744    0.826
     y3                1.032    0.014   71.723    0.000    0.791    0.847
     y4                0.810    0.010   80.275    0.000    0.620    0.715
     y5                0.790    0.014   55.596    0.000    0.605    0.714
     y6                0.837    0.014   57.822    0.000    0.641    0.728

while plain ML gives

 > fitb <- sem('f =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5 + y6', data = jdat2,
estimator = "ML", meanstructure = TRUE)
 > summary(fitb, standardized = TRUE)
lavaan (0.5-20) converged normally after  20 iterations

   Number of observations                         10000

   Estimator                                         ML
   Minimum Function Test Statistic            10106.617
   Degrees of freedom                                 9
   P-value (Chi-square)                           0.000

Parameter Estimates:

   Information                                 Expected
   Standard Errors                             Standard

Latent Variables:
                    Estimate  Std.Err  Z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
   f =~
     y1                1.000                               0.725    0.731
     y2                1.005    0.016   64.557    0.000    0.729    0.727
     y3                1.015    0.016   65.021    0.000    0.736    0.733
     y4                0.811    0.015   53.110    0.000    0.589    0.589
     y5                0.815    0.015   53.309    0.000    0.591    0.591
     y6                0.816    0.015   53.430    0.000    0.592    0.592

The 'upward' bias we observe in the factor loadings is largely due to a
'downward' bias in the estimation of the residual variances of the
(continuous) y-indicators. 2nd order estimators (closed-form marginal
ML, DWLS, ULS) can happily ignore the fourth-order moments, and adjust
these residual variances freely to optimize fit. The WLS method does not
have this luxury, and must obey the fourth-moment patterns as found in
the data.

I do agree there is not much literature discussing this, at least not in
the SEM context.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
You have a complex nonrecursive structuralmodel,with many reciprocal relationships.  When A predicts B and B predicts A, you usually need at least one of the two to have its own predictor, unshared with the other in the pair.  But you don't just have pairs--you have tangles of reciprocal relations.  You will need to learn about the rank and order conditions for identification of structural models.  Bollen (1989) in his classic Structural Equations with Latent Variables, actually presents a very readable treatment.
     Lots of DF does not protect you from identification problems.  Nonnegative DF is a necessary but not sufficient condition for identification.
     I agree with you that Warning 1 is not the central cause of your problem. However, strange numbers can result from that "outlier variance" condition.  I would suggest rescaling--say, dividing that variable by 10 or by 100--to take that issue off the table, too.

messages.body_plain:
Jason--
    I think the core of your identification problem (which is probably the source of the "can't estimate standard errors" warning) is in your structural model:

> + #Regressions
> +   OInno ~ WE + EIS
> +   ODev ~ WE + EIS
> + #Intercepts
> + #Variances
> +   WE ~~ EIS + OInno + ODev + Stra + Ven
> +   EIS ~~ OInno + ODev + Stra + Ven

You have WE and EIS predicted by OInno and ODev, but then you allow WE and EIS to share residual covariance with OInno and ODev.  That makes your structural model nonrecursive and raises potential identification issues.  If you did not allow these particular residual covariances, then I think your identification problem would disappear.  If you want to retain these residual covariances, then you are going to need to learn something about identification.
     I don't know whether the negative residual covariances are related to the "not positive definite" message.  Covariances can certainly be negative--though one badly placed negative in a covariance matrix can certainly make a matrix not positive definite.
--Ed Rigdon

On 12/13/2015 05:58 PM, Maya Abou Zeid wrote:
> Thank you for the follow-up. Yes, the NA is still there with the new

You get NA values (and a warning explaining why) if you have negative
variances.

> I would also like to check with you a couple of things. My model
> includes ordered indicators. For the corresponding continuous latent
> response variable (y*), as I understand, the variance of its error term
> should be 1 for identification purposes.

By default, lavaan will constrain the (total) variance of y* to be one.
The residual variance of y*, then, is not a free parameter, but a
function of other model parameters.

See:

Muthen, B. (1978). Contributions to factor analysis of dichotomous
variables. Psychometrika, 43, 551-560.
(http://www.statmodel.com/download/ContributionsToFactorAnalysis.pdf)

Equation 4 (page 552) shows how the (diagonal) elements of 'Psi'
(corresponding with the residual variances of the observed variables)
are a function of other model parameters. (Note: this is for a model
without a structural component)

For the multiple group setting, read this:

Muthen, B., & Christoffersson, A. (1981). Simultaneous factor analysis
of dichotomous variables in several groups. Psychometrika, 46(4), 407-419.

Next, read this webnote to understand the difference between 'delta' and
'theta' parameterization, and the role of the Delta scaling parameters:

http://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

> I estimate the model on two datasets separately. But when I combine the
> datasets and use multi-group analysis (with equality constraints on the
> structural equation parameters and on intercepts and thresholds in the

This (default) behavior certainly is as intended. Residuals between
outcome variables (either latent or observed) are -per default- always
correlated. In the defaults-avoiding lavaan() function, this is
controlled by the auto.cov.y= argument (see table 3 in the JSS paper).

You can always 'identify' those outcome variables as follows:

 > PT <- lavaanify(CQmodel5, auto = TRUE)
 > lavNames(PT, "lv.y")
[1] "MCQ" "CCQ" "BCQ"

(and using "ov.y" for the observed ones).

I believe most multivariate software behaves like this (by default),
including Mplus. The idea is just like in multivariate regression: we do
not -by default- impose a structure on the residuals of outcome
variables. We assume their covariance structure is unstructured, unless
we have theoretical reasons to impose another structure (eg compound
symmetry or AR(1) if the outcomes are repeated measures).

If you are using the sem/cfa function, and you wish to override this,
you need to do this in the syntax, by adding lines like

MCQ ~~ 0*CCQ

if you prefer a zero residual covariance.

Yves.

Your scaling correction factor is quite large at 3.40--I have not seen one so large in a long time.  I would guess that you have highly kurtotic data.  You will want to understand the nature of your data--what is driving this extremely large scaling factor.
     You have 37 observed variables and 6 common factors.  Your n is not terribly small for such a model, but it is not at all large.  You want to review the formulas for alternative fit indices like CFI and RMSEA.  As soon as chi-square is smaller than DF, CFI = 1 and RMSEA = exactly.  The TLI above 1.00 might be taken as a sign of overfitting, though you appear to have only 6 common factors and no free residual covariances.
   My advice would be to report the original and robust chi-squares, and the scaling factor, then report the alternative fit indices that go with the robust chi-square.  But you will want to explain how your data earned such a large scaling factor, and also report enough about the parameter estimates so that someone could replicate your analysis.  One way to obtain a good fit is to use weak items with low correlations.  That would be consistent with the rather small baseline model chi-square after scaling correction, again given that your model has 37 observed variables. You will want to show reviewers that this is not the case with your research.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I wanted to get some feedback on the appropriateness of my approach. I am running multigroup confirmatory factor analysis models on ordinal data from a 15 item scale with three response categories. The most restrictive model consists of an invariance constraint on the loadings and thresholds. I am wanting to supply my own independence model to ensure the estimated CFIs are indeed generated from nested models. In keeping with the guidance provided by Widamin and Thompson (2003), I constructed my own independence model consisting of requests for estimated variances and thresholds with an invariance constraint on the thresholds (see syntax below). I think what I am concerned about the most is whether I have correctly specified my independence model using lavaan syntax. The concern I am experiencing stems from the novelty of the task for me but also because in the independence model output the y* variances are equal to 1 in group 1 as expected, but diverge slightly from 1  in the second group under the 'Estimate' column (.898 is the largest value in terms of deviation) - I expected y* to equal 1 for both groups. I don't know if I am all that concerned about it because y* variances are equal to 1 in both groups under Std.all, and that seems to make sense to me. It is just inconsistent with the output from the models of substantive interest where the variances for y* are equal 1 in both groups under the 'Estimate' column. I am thinking the difference stems from differences in scaling constraints between the substantive models and independence model owing to the loadings being fixed at zero in the independence model. In which case, I would assume my independence model is fine but thought I better confer with folks smarter than I.

messages.body_plain:
> I don't understand why the latent variances for group 2 need to be freed in the weak invariance model. What is accomplished by doing this?

The only reason you fix the latent variances to 1 is to set an arbitrary scale for the latent construct.  It doesn't have to be the same -- you could fix it to 1 in the first group and 2 in the second group, but you probably don't have any reason to do that.  The only way to estimate from the data whether the latent variances differ across groups is to assume a 1-unit change in the latent variable produces the same amount of change (lambda) in an indicator for both groups, which corresponds to weak-invariance constraints on factor loadings.  If you constrain the factor loadings to equality without freeing the latent variances in all but 1 group (for scale-identification), then you are not testing weak invariance alone, but rather 2 hypotheses that should be treated independently: (a) are the factor loadings the same and (b) are the latent variances the same.  There is no theoretical reason to test both of those hypotheses in a single step.

Terry
